lessons.title: Half-caste: voice, performance and identity
lessons.bigQuestion: How can the form of a poem challenge the way people are labelled?
objectives: Analyse how Agard uses non-standard spelling, humour and direct address
Explain how the poem challenges the term 'half-caste'
Compare Half-caste with Search For My Tongue
successCriteria: All: identify the poem's attitude to the term 'half-caste'
Most: analyse the effect of non-standard language
Some: compare two poets' methods of presenting identity
lessons.crossCurricular: Arabic: language, accent and identity; Music/Art: examples Agard uses (Picasso, Tchaikovsky)
lessons.smsc: Moral: dignity of all people (karamah); Spiritual: Surah al-Hujurat 49:13, that humanity was made into peoples and tribes to know one another

keywords.def: language that departs from the standard written form, such as dialect or Creole
a language formed from a mix of languages, spoken in the Caribbean and elsewhere
speaking straight to the reader or listener
poetry written to be spoken aloud
a fixed and unfair idea about a group

starter: Bismillah. What is the effect of direct address?
Define 'dialect'.
Which technique did Bhatt use to show identity in her poem?

teach.heading: A sensitive and important poem
bullets: John Agard, born in Guyana, moved to Britain in 1977
The poem targets the term 'half-caste'
Agard writes in Creole-influenced spelling
The speaker argues each person is whole
teach.note: TEACHER: supply Half-caste (John Agard) from the licensed anthology. 'Half-caste' is an outdated and offensive term; it appears only because the poem challenges it. Remind pupils to use the word only when quoting and analysing, and to treat the topic with respect. Remind them that this is a poem about dignity: link to the Qur'anic idea (Surah al-Hujurat 49:13) that human diversity exists so people may know one another, and that nobility lies in righteousness, not appearance. Agard is a Guyanese-born poet and performer; the poem is meant to be performed.

teach.heading: Voice, spelling and humour
teach.note: The speaker uses everyday examples (such as art and music) to show that mixing makes something richer, not lesser. Ask pupils how the Creole-influenced spelling ('yu', 'wha', 'mih') changes how we hear the poem and who the speaker is. Ask: what is the tone: angry, playful, or both?

right.title: What he argues
points: A person is a whole human being

teach.heading: Model: language as resistance
teach.note: I do. Notice how the paragraph links the spelling to the speaker's cultural identity, and then to the poem's argument. Ask pupils to read the phrase aloud in the voice of the poem.

model.problem: How does Agard use language to challenge prejudice in Half-caste?
steps: Point: he uses non-standard spelling to give the speaker a confident, distinct voice.
Evidence: the demand 'Explain yuself'.
Zoom: the imperative and the Creole-influenced spelling put the speaker in charge and force the listener to justify the label.
Link: the poem shows that a language form can be as valid as standard English.
model.answer: Agard gives the speaker a confident voice through non-standard spelling. The demand 'Explain yuself' is an imperative, which makes the speaker, not the listener, the one in control, while the spelling asserts that this way of speaking is valid. The language form is therefore part of the poem's argument against prejudice.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Discuss why D is wrong: the humour is part of the argument. The poem is playful but serious.

check.q: Why does Agard end by inviting the listener to return with 'de whole of yu eye'?
options: To be polite.
To suggest that to understand someone you must give them your whole attention and respect.
To say that the speaker will leave.
To make the poem rhyme.
check.why: The ending turns the poem's argument back on the listener: they must see whole people. The other options do not fit the tone or meaning.

teach.heading: Compare: Half-caste and Search For My Tongue
bullets: Both explore language and identity
Agard: confrontational and performed
Bhatt: reflective and personal
Both let language appear on the page as itself
teach.note: Plan a quick AO3 link. Pupils find one similarity (language as identity) and one difference (public argument versus private journey). Remind them to link methods as well as ideas.

practice: Retrieve: define 'direct address'.
Name two features of a dramatic monologue.
What is a stereotype?
independent: Core: write a paragraph on the effect of non-standard spelling.
Extend: write a paragraph on how Agard uses examples.
Stretch: write a comparison paragraph between Half-caste and Search For My Tongue.
exit: What does the poem argue?
Name one method and its effect.
Big question: how can a poem's form challenge the way people are labelled?
lessons.homework: Write a comparison paragraph (about 120 words) on identity in Half-caste and Search For My Tongue.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-teach the word 'caste' and 'dialect' with sensitivity; provide the model's sentence frames. EAL pupils may share how accents and languages feel in their own lives. Stretch: research performance poetry and compare the written and spoken versions.

lessons.title: Death and memory: Do not go gentle, Remember and Poem at Thirty-Nine
lessons.bigQuestion: How do poets speak to someone they will lose, and what do they want from them?
objectives: Analyse the villanelle form of Do not go gentle into that good night
Analyse the Petrarchan structure of Remember
Apply the method to Poem at Thirty-Nine and compare the three
successCriteria: All: identify who speaks to whom in each poem
Most: analyse form in two poems
Some: compare the speakers' requests
lessons.crossCurricular: Islamic Studies: remembering the dead and du'a; History: Victorian attitudes to mourning
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: remembrance of the deceased and making du'a; Moral: honouring parents

keywords.def: a 19-line poem with two repeating refrains
a repeated line
a 14-line poem of an octave and a sestet
the first eight lines of a Petrarchan sonnet
the final six lines of a Petrarchan sonnet

starter: Bismillah. What is a volta?
What two parts form a Petrarchan sonnet?
Name a poem in the anthology addressed to a loved one.

teach.heading: Do not go gentle: a son's command
bullets: Dylan Thomas, 1951
A villanelle: two refrains repeat
The speaker urges a dying father to resist
Wise, good, wild and grave men all resist
teach.note: TEACHER: supply Do not go gentle into that good night (Dylan Thomas). The poem was written for Thomas's dying father. The villanelle form, with its two repeating lines, makes the plea sound like an obsessive, desperate chant. The refrain 'Rage, rage against the dying of the light' is the emotional peak. The poem ends on a direct plea for his father's 'fierce tears'. Ask: what does the speaker want his father to do, and why? Note that the speaker commands but also begs.

teach.heading: Remember: a gentle request
teach.note: Remember (Christina Rossetti) is a Petrarchan sonnet: the octave asks to be remembered, the sestet turns ('Yet if you should forget me for a while') and says that it is better to forget and smile than to remember and be sad. Compare tone: Thomas demands, Rossetti permits. Ask pupils to say which request is more selfless and why. Context: Rossetti wrote the poem as a young woman; she was a devout Anglican and wrote often about love and death. Do not guess at biography beyond this.

left.title: Do not go gentle
points: Speaker fears loss and wants resistance

right.title: Remember
points: Gentle request, then permission to forget
Speaker values the loved one's happiness

teach.heading: Model: contrasting requests
teach.note: I do. Show how a link sentence can use a pair of quotations. Ask: which poem would comfort a mourner more?

model.problem: Compare how each speaker addresses the person they will lose.
steps: Point: both speakers address a loved one, but make opposite requests.
Evidence: Thomas demands 'Rage, rage', Rossetti allows 'forget and smile'.
Zoom: the repeated imperative creates urgency and defiance, while the gentle permission shows selfless love.
Link: the villanelle's repetition suits the first, whereas the sonnet's turn suits the second.
model.answer: Both speakers address a loved one but make opposite requests. Thomas commands 'Rage, rage', and the repeated imperative creates urgent defiance, whereas Rossetti's speaker permits the listener to 'forget and smile', which reveals a selfless love. The villanelle's insistent refrains suit Thomas's desperation, but the sonnet's turn allows Rossetti's gentle change of heart.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Use the quick vote. The common error is B: the poem is addressed to the father, not a general reader.

check.q: Why does Thomas use a villanelle?
options: Because villanelles are about death.
The repeating refrains create an obsessive, pleading chant that suits his desperate plea.
To show he is a wise man.
Because the poem is about nature.
check.why: The repetition mirrors his refusal to let go. A is untrue as a rule; C and D do not account for the form's effect.

teach.heading: Poem at Thirty-Nine: apply the method
bullets: Alice Walker, an American poet and novelist
A speaker reflects on her father
Ask: who speaks, to whom, in what form?
Teacher supplies the text
teach.note: TEACHER: supply Poem at Thirty-Nine (Alice Walker) from the licensed anthology; do not rely on memory of its details. This is a method slide: have pupils annotate voice, address, tone, structure and what the speaker learns about her father and herself. Then compare to Do not go gentle and Remember: all three poems are about family or love and loss. Ask: does the speaker seem to be accepting, resisting, or rediscovering?

practice: Retrieve: define 'refrain' and 'octave'.
Which poem so far has an unusual rhyme scheme and why?
What do du'a for the deceased remind us about remembrance?
independent: Core: write a paragraph on the villanelle form.
Extend: write a paragraph on the volta in Remember.
Stretch: write a three-way comparison plan (Thomas, Rossetti, Walker) of how each poet addresses loss.
exit: Name the form of Remember.
What does the refrain in Thomas's poem do?
Big question: how do poets speak to someone they will lose?
lessons.homework: Write a comparison paragraph (about 120 words) on the tone of Do not go gentle and Remember.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a form map (villanelle and sonnet) with colour-coded refrains. EAL pupils can add their own family terms. Stretch: compare with a favourite elegy from your own reading.

Write a comparative introduction and body paragraph
Use timing and a checklist

a word that links ideas
the central argument of an essay
make a judgement about how well something works
a short quotation woven into a sentence

starter: Bismillah. List the four parts of a comparison paragraph.
Which two AOs does Section B assess?

teach.heading: The question and the clock
bullets: 30 marks, about 40 minutes
A choice of two questions
Read both, then choose carefully
5 minutes plan, 30 writing, 5 checking
teach.note: Remind pupils the exam supplies a clean copy of the poems. Check the latest past papers or specimen paper for the precise stems and the AO2/AO3 split, which was not confirmed when this scheme was written. An example (original) question for practice: 'Compare how poets present the effects of time on people in Remember and one other poem from Part 3 of the anthology.' Ask pupils how they would choose the second poem: one that offers strong links in theme and contrasting methods.

teach.heading: The plan: a comparison grid
teach.note: Teach a grid of three rows (idea/theme, methods, effect) and two columns (poem A, poem B). Pupils fill it with short quotations. The point of the plan is to prevent writing two separate essays. Use the table as a template and show a filled example.

teach.heading: Model: introduction and linked paragraph
teach.note: I do. Read the answer aloud. Point out the thesis in the introduction, the comparing connective, and the short quotations embedded in sentences. Ask: where is AO2? Where is AO3?

model.problem: Compare how poets present the effects of time on people in Remember and one other poem.
steps: Introduction: state a clear comparison thesis in one or two sentences.
Paragraph: point, linked evidence from both poems.
Zoom: explain a language or form feature in each.
Link: end with a judgement about contrasting attitudes.
model.answer: Rossetti and Thomas both present time as a force that takes loved ones, but respond differently. In Remember, the gentle 'forget and smile' accepts the passing of time peacefully, whereas Thomas's commanding 'Rage, rage' refuses to accept it. The sonnet's turn shows Rossetti's gradual acceptance, while the villanelle's refrains trap Thomas in his defiance.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Ask pupils to rank A to D from weakest to strongest. A and C separate poems; D has a vague claim.

check.q: Which opening sentence is strongest for a comparison?
options: Remember is a sonnet by Rossetti.
Rossetti accepts loss gently, whereas Thomas fights it fiercely.
Both poems are about death.
Poets use many techniques.
check.why: B states a clear comparison with both poets. A is a single-poem fact, C is too general, D has no content.

teach.heading: Checklist for marks
bullets: Short quotations embedded in sentences
Methods named and explained
Links every paragraph, not only at the end
Conclude with a judgement
teach.note: Give a checklist for self-assessment. Remind pupils that AO3 is about connections, so each paragraph should link the poems, not just the conclusion. If time allows, pupils peer-mark a paragraph with two stars and a wish.

practice: Retrieve: three connectives for similarity and three for contrast.
Write one embedded quotation from any poem you know.
What is the danger of writing about poem A for half and then poem B?

Extend: write the introduction and one body paragraph.
Stretch: write a conclusion that makes a judgement.
exit: How many minutes for planning?
Write one linking sentence.

Spot language, form and structure features and explain their effects
Write one analytical paragraph on an unseen poem

Some: trace a shift in tone or structure across the poem

keywords.def: a text you have not studied before
language that creates pictures or sensations
the writer's attitude or mood
how a poem is organised from start to end
a turn in thought or mood

starter: Bismillah. What does AO2 reward?
List three language techniques with an effect for each.
What is the difference between form and structure?

teach.heading: What the 20 marks reward
bullets: One 20-mark question on an unseen poem
AO2: language, form and structure and their effects
Closed book, no prepared quotations
Spend about 30 minutes
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Explain that the unseen poem rewards method, not memory. The spec lists AO2 for this section. Ask pupils what a poem that they have never seen cannot be: it cannot be memorised, so we practise a method that works on any poem. TEACHER: also supply the school's chosen selection of modern poems that the spec says candidates study to prepare; this scheme does not name them.

teach.heading: A five-step method
teach.note: Teach the cycle and then practise it. 1 Read twice (first for gist, second for detail). 2 Ask: who speaks, to whom, about what, and what changes? 3 Annotate: techniques with effects. 4 Plan three points, one per part of the poem. 5 Write, using short quotations. Emphasise that the second read is where pupils notice the turn.

teach.heading: Our poem (original, written for TGA)
teach.note: Read aloud. This poem was written for the school, so it can be shown in full. Ask pupils to read it twice and to complete the first two steps. Possible answers: a lonely or reflective speaker on a night bus; a shift at the end from emptiness to a gentle, almost hopeful image. Guide, do not tell.

quote.text:
The last bus hums through the rain's grey hush,
its windows lit like a row of small rooms.
I watch my own face, thin in the glass,
float over the shuttered shops.

Nobody speaks. A man folds a newspaper
smaller and smaller, as if to disappear in it.
The driver's radio murmurs the weather
to no one, and the wipers keep their count.

At my stop the doors sigh open.
Cold stands on the step like a patient dog.
I step down into the dark, and behind me
the bus goes on, a lantern carrying its strangers.
quote.source: Original practice poem, 'Last Bus', written for Tarbiyyah Global Academy

teach.heading: Model: one analytical paragraph
teach.note: I do. Highlight how the analysis begins with an idea, not a technique, and zooms into one word. The final sentence ties the image to the poem's overall mood. Note it also gives a tentative alternative reading.

model.problem: How does the poet present the speaker's experience of the journey?
steps: Point: the poet presents the journey as lonely but quietly comforting.
Evidence: windows 'lit like a row of small rooms'.
Zoom: the simile turns the bus into a series of separate rooms, so passengers seem isolated even though they share a space; the soft word 'small' suggests vulnerability.
Link: the final image of a 'lantern' gives the strangers a kind of warmth.
model.answer: The poet presents the journey as lonely but quietly comforting. The simile 'lit like a row of small rooms' turns the bus into separate, private spaces, so that the passengers seem isolated even though they share a journey. The word 'small' hints at their vulnerability, but the final image of a 'lantern' adds warmth, suggesting the strangers are carried together through the dark.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Quick vote. Ask which sentence explains an effect. A names a technique only, C guesses at the season, and D simply repeats the quotation.

check.q: Which sentence is the best AO2 analysis of 'Cold stands on the step like a patient dog'?
options: The poet uses a simile.
The simile personifies the cold as a waiting animal, making the weather seem alive and patient, which adds menace and companionship.
The poem was probably written in winter.
The cold is cold.
check.why: B names the technique, quotes an idea and explains an effect. A names a technique only; C guesses; D is circular.

teach.heading: Structure: where does the poem turn?
bullets: Stanza 1: setting and reflection
Stanza 2: strangers, silence
Stanza 3: leaving the bus
Look for shifts in tone or image
teach.note: Pupils annotate how each stanza has a different focus. Ask: what changes from first to last? Likely answer: from looking inwards (own reflection) to looking back at the bus with warmth. Remind pupils structure is part of AO2 and always worth a comment.

practice: As a class, circle every verb in the first stanza of 'Last Bus'. What do they suggest?
In pairs, find a place where the poet uses personification.
Why might the poet end with 'strangers' rather than 'people'?
independent: Core: write one analytical paragraph on stanza 2 using the model.
Extend: add a paragraph on the ending.
Stretch: write a short paragraph on structure across the three stanzas.
exit: List the five steps of the method.
Write a technique and an effect from 'Last Bus'.
Big question: how can you analyse a poem you have never read?
lessons.homework: Practise steps 1-3 of the method on a poem of your choice from the school's modern poetry selection and bring your annotations.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a pre-annotated copy with technique labels and a glossary (shuttered, murmurs, lantern). Allow oral rehearsal. Stretch: rewrite one line in plain language and discuss what is lost.

lessons.title: Unseen poetry: planning and writing a 20-mark response under time
lessons.bigQuestion: How do you structure a whole unseen response so that every paragraph earns AO2 marks?
objectives: Plan a full unseen response in ten minutes
Write an introduction and three developed paragraphs
Self-assess using a checklist
successCriteria: All: plan three points with quotations
Most: write three analytical paragraphs
Some: write a conclusion that evaluates the poet's overall effect
lessons.crossCurricular: English Language: structuring an extended answer
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty and humility in reading closely

keywords.def: focus on a single word or phrase for detailed analysis
a sentence that states the main idea of a paragraph
make a judgement about how effective something is
words like 'suggests' and 'perhaps' that show careful reading
a change of mood or viewpoint

starter: Bismillah. List the five steps of the unseen method.
Give three tentative verbs for analysis.
Name one structural feature you can comment on.

teach.heading: Reading the poem and the question
bullets: Read the question first
Then read the poem twice
Underline words in the question
Ask: what is this question steering me to?
teach.note: Introduce the practice question: 'How does the poet present the speaker's feelings about the grandmother in this poem?' (original). Show how to underline 'how', 'present' and 'feelings', which steer pupils to methods and mood. Remind them that the examiners credit the way the poem is written, not a story retelling.

teach.heading: Practice poem (original)
teach.note: Read the poem aloud. Pupils complete steps 1 and 2 individually in silence for two minutes, then pair share. Ask: what is the speaker's attitude towards the grandmother at the start, and does it change? (Likely answer: admiration and tenderness, then regret at his own impatience, then a hopeful, affectionate memory.)

quote.text:
She kneaded the dough as if it owed her something,
her knuckles knotted like the roots of the old fig tree.
Flour rose around her, a small weather of its own,
and the radio sang in a language she kept for kitchens.

I was told to watch. I watched the heel of her palm
push, fold, turn; push, fold, turn.
No recipe. Only a patience older than the house.

Now my own hands, pale and quick, rush the work.
The dough sulks. It sticks. It will not rise.
Somewhere she is shaking her head, and smiling,
and saying, slowly, again.
quote.source: Original practice poem, 'Grandmother's Hands', written for Tarbiyyah Global Academy

teach.heading: Model: planning in ten minutes
teach.note: I do. Show how the plan has three points following the poem's order (beginning, turn, ending), each with one quotation and one effect. Remind pupils this is not an essay about stories: every point needs an effect.

model.problem: Plan a response to: How does the poet present the speaker's feelings about the grandmother?
steps: Point 1 (stanza 1): admiration; 'knuckles knotted like the roots' shows strength and age.
Point 2 (stanza 2): respect for her skill; 'push, fold, turn' has a steady rhythm of patience.
Point 3 (stanza 3): regret and love; 'The dough sulks' personifies the speaker's frustration.
Conclusion: the poem ends with affection as the grandmother's voice is imagined.
model.answer: A plan with three points that follow the poem's order and each include a short quotation and an effect, then a brief conclusion.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Reveal the answer and discuss why A is too narrow. Remind pupils to use a range of examples across the poem, not only the first stanza.

check.q: Which plan gives the best coverage?
options: Three points all from stanza 1.
One point from the beginning, one from the turn at 'Now', and one from the ending.
A summary of the story in order.
A list of every technique in the poem.
check.why: B follows the poem's structure and includes the turn. A neglects the rest; C and D lack analysis.

teach.heading: Checklist and timing
bullets: 5 minutes: read and annotate
5 minutes: plan
20 minutes: write
Check: effects explained? Structure covered?
teach.note: Give the self-assessment checklist: Did I use short quotations? Did I explain an effect each time? Did I comment on structure or form? Did I use tentative language? Remind pupils the paper has other sections so about 30 minutes is realistic. In a timed task, circulate and prompt pupils who retell the poem.

practice: Retrieve: why is 'the poet uses a metaphor' not enough for AO2?
Name three verbs that show careful, tentative reading.
What is personification?
independent: Core: write an introduction and two body paragraphs for the practice question.
Extend: complete the third paragraph and a conclusion.
Stretch: write a paragraph that evaluates how the shift at 'Now' changes the poem's mood.
exit: What should you underline in the question?
Write one tentative analytical sentence.
Big question: how do you structure a response so every paragraph earns AO2 marks?
lessons.homework: Complete the timed response in full, or write the best two paragraphs, then self-assess against the checklist.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a paragraph frame (The poet presents... through... This suggests...). Give extra time if agreed. Stretch: compare your response with a partner and improve one sentence each.

lessons.title: Modern prose: reading the question and building an argument (AO1)
lessons.bigQuestion: How do you turn knowledge of a novel into an argument about its themes and characters?
objectives: Unpick the Section C question and choose between two
Build a theme-based argument with short, precise evidence
Explain how AO1 differs from retelling the plot
successCriteria: All: identify the focus of the question
Most: plan three points with evidence
Some: make an informed personal judgement
lessons.crossCurricular: History: the American Great Depression (Of Mice and Men); PSHE: loneliness and community
lessons.smsc: Social: friendship, loneliness and the duty to care for the weak

keywords.def: a central idea explored in a text
a person in a story, built from words and actions
a short quotation or reference that supports a point
an informed, original response to the text
a clear line of reasoning that runs through an essay

starter: Bismillah. What does AO1 reward?
Name a theme in a novel you know and one scene that shows it.
Why is summary not analysis?

teach.heading: The Section C question
bullets: One 40-mark question from two
AO1 (close knowledge, personal engagement) and AO4 (context)
Closed book: learn short, flexible quotations
About 45 minutes
teach.note: TEACHER: this lesson is text-neutral; models use Of Mice and Men (Steinbeck, 1937), so adapt them to the class's chosen text. The prose options on the spec are To Kill a Mockingbird, Of Mice and Men, The Whale Rider, The Joy Luck Club, Things Fall Apart, Klara and the Sun and Western Lane; the last two are new, with first assessment in May 2026, so check the latest past papers and sample materials. The school must supply the class set of the chosen novel. Examiners' reports show questions on theme, character and significance, so train pupils to read the key words in any question.

teach.heading: Option table: what to know for any novel
teach.note: Use the table to build a one-page knowledge organiser for your chosen text. Pupils fill in the same headings for their novel.

head: Text
Narrator or voice
Setting
A central idea
rows: Love and what makes us human

teach.heading: Model: a developed argument paragraph
teach.note: I do. The phrase 'loneliest guys in the world' is George's, early in the novel; 'A guy needs somebody' is Crooks in chapter 4. Check against the class copy before use. Show how the paragraph begins with a claim, then evidence, then analysis, then a link to the whole text.

model.problem: Explore how Steinbeck presents loneliness in Of Mice and Men.
steps: Point: Steinbeck presents loneliness as the defining condition of ranch workers.
Evidence: George says they are 'the loneliest guys in the world'.
Zoom: the superlative makes isolation sound universal, and the plain 'guys' shows the speaker's rough, unsentimental voice; the later line from Crooks, 'A guy needs somebody', gives the cure.
Link: the shared dream of the farm is the novel's answer to loneliness, but it is never reached.
model.answer: Steinbeck presents loneliness as the defining condition of ranch workers. George's superlative, the 'loneliest guys in the world', makes isolation sound universal, and the plain language of 'guys' reflects the unsentimental voice of men who rarely speak of feeling. Crooks later admits 'A guy needs somebody', which suggests that friendship is a basic human need. The shared dream of the farm is the novel's answer to loneliness, but its failure leaves the reader with a sense of tragedy.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Ask pupils to defend their choice. B is the best because it gives an argument and an effect; D describes the plot.

check.q: Which opening sentence is best for the question 'Explore the theme of loneliness'?
options: George and Lennie go to a ranch.
Steinbeck presents loneliness as a force that shapes every character's choices.
Loneliness is a theme in many books.
Lennie likes rabbits.
check.why: B states a clear argument. A and D retell the plot, and C is too general.

teach.heading: Planning the whole answer
bullets: Introduction: a clear argument
Three paragraphs: beginning, middle, end of the text
Short quotations, often a few words
Conclusion: a considered personal view
teach.note: Show a plan: one paragraph from early in the text, one from the middle, one from the end, then a conclusion. Stress personal engagement: an informed opinion about what the writer wants us to feel or think. Note: context (AO4) comes in the next lesson.

practice: Retrieve: name three themes in your set text.
Write a short quotation from your text and its meaning.
What is the difference between a point and a retelling?
independent: Core: complete the knowledge organiser for your text.
Extend: plan three points for 'Explore how the writer presents friendship (or family)'.
Stretch: write one paragraph with a link to the whole text.
exit: What does AO1 reward?
Write the first sentence of an argument about your text.
Big question: how do you turn knowledge of a novel into an argument?
lessons.homework: Choose one theme in your text and write a 150-word paragraph using the model structure.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a character and theme word bank and a paragraph frame. Pair EAL pupils with a reading partner. Stretch: argue whether a different theme could be central to the novel.

lessons.title: Modern prose: using context (AO4) without bolting it on
lessons.bigQuestion: How does knowing when and where a novel was written help you understand what it says?
objectives: Explain what AO4 rewards
Link a context point to a writer's choice
Choose context that is relevant to the text and the question
successCriteria: All: state one context fact for your text
Most: link a context fact to a quotation
Some: explain how context shapes the writer's purpose
lessons.crossCurricular: History: Jim Crow and the American South; British colonialism in Africa; the Depression
lessons.smsc: Moral: justice, dignity and human rights; Social: empathy for people in different times and places

keywords.def: the circumstances in which a text was written or set
why a writer wrote something
an unfair opinion formed without good reason
when one country takes control of another
a context fact stuck on without a link to the text

starter: Bismillah. What is AO4?
Give two reasons why a writer might write a novel.
Why does a 'bolt-on' fact fail to earn marks?

teach.heading: What AO4 asks for
bullets: Understanding of relationships between texts and contexts
Context of writing and context of setting
Always link to the writer's choices
Never a history lecture
teach.note: Explain that context can mean when and why the text was written, the world it describes and how it was received. Marks come from showing how this context helps explain something in the text. A bolt-on is a fact with no link, such as 'The Great Depression began in 1929' with no mention of the novel. TEACHER: tell pupils to use only the context for their set text; the table below is a revision guide for the options and should be checked against standard references.

teach.heading: Context table for the options
teach.note: Use this as a summary only: check facts against reliable sources and the class text. For Klara and the Sun, a context point is the rapid development of artificial intelligence and gene-editing, which the novel imagines. For Western Lane, the context is a British Gujarati family dealing with grief in a world of competitive sport. Do not overstate.

head: Text
Context of setting or writing
Link to the text

Igbo society and colonial rule; published 1958
Tradition tested by a girl leader
Chinese immigrants in the USA; published 1989
Questions about love and being human

teach.heading: Model: context linked to a choice
teach.note: I do. Read the quotation in the class text and confirm its place. Stress how the context sentence explains why the writer made a choice and how it affects the reader. Atticus's advice appears in chapter 3.

model.problem: How does Harper Lee use context to shape the reader's view of prejudice?
steps: Point: she presents prejudice as built into the world of Maycomb.
Evidence: Atticus says you must 'climb into his skin and walk around in it'.
Zoom: set in a segregated 1930s town, the novel shows that empathy was rare; published in 1960 as the civil rights movement grew, Lee asks readers to see beyond skin colour.
Link: Scout's child perspective makes the injustice feel plain and wrong.
model.answer: Lee presents prejudice as built into the world of Maycomb. Atticus's advice that you must 'climb into his skin and walk around in it' stresses empathy, a rare quality in a segregated 1930s town. Because the novel was published in 1960, as the civil rights movement grew, Lee seems to ask her readers to look beyond skin colour. Scout's child perspective makes the injustice seem plain and wrong.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Ask pupils to rank the statements. C is the model: context is explicit and linked. A and B are bolt-ons.

options: Slavery ended in 1865.
The author was born in 1926.
Racial segregation in 1930s Alabama explains why Tom Robinson cannot expect a fair trial, which Lee uses to condemn injustice.
Many people were prejudiced.
check.why: Only C links a context fact to the text and to the writer's purpose. A and B are bolt-ons, D is vague.

teach.heading: Choose context that fits the question
bullets: Read the question: which context helps?
One or two precise context points per paragraph
Link to a short quotation each time
Do not force context where it does not fit
teach.note: Teach selective use: in a question about family, one context point about family structure is more helpful than a general history paragraph. Pupils practise by writing a context sentence for each of three quotations from their text. Mention that context can be woven into analysis in the same sentence.

practice: Retrieve: define 'context' and 'purpose'.
Name two factors that shape an author's choices.
What is a bolt-on?
independent: Core: write three context sentences for your text, each linked to a quotation.
Extend: write a full paragraph with context woven in.
Stretch: explain how a different context (e.g. a modern reader) changes the response.
exit: Which sentence uses context well?
Write one link between a context fact and a writer's choice.
Big question: how does context help you understand what a novel says?
lessons.homework: Research one context fact for your text from a reliable source and write a linked paragraph (about 120 words).
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a timeline of the text's period and visual support. Pre-teach 'segregation', 'colonial'. Stretch: evaluate whether the writer's context limits the novel's message today.

lessons.title: Writing the 40-mark prose essay: planning, paragraphs and timing
lessons.bigQuestion: What does a high-level 40-mark essay on a novel look like?
objectives: Plan a Section C essay in ten minutes
Write a developed paragraph with evidence, analysis and context
Review and improve using a mark-scheme style checklist
successCriteria: All: plan an essay with three points
Most: write two developed paragraphs
Some: write a full essay with a considered conclusion
lessons.crossCurricular: English Language: extended writing under time pressure
lessons.smsc: Moral: fairness and balance in argument

keywords.def: the final part of an essay that sums up your argument
the first sentence of a paragraph stating its point
weave a quotation into your own sentence
a reasoned conclusion about the text
why something matters in the text as a whole

starter: Bismillah. What does AO4 reward and how do you show it?
Give one short quotation and use it in a sentence.
What is a topic sentence?

teach.heading: The plan
bullets: Read both questions; choose one in two minutes
Plan: argument, three points, quotations, context
Use the text's beginning, middle and end
Leave 5 minutes to check
teach.note: TEACHER: model with Things Fall Apart (Achebe, 1958); adapt to the class's chosen text. Example original question: 'Explore how Achebe presents fear in Things Fall Apart.' Show how to turn this into a claim and three evidence points. Remind pupils that for 40 marks they have about 45 minutes, so developed paragraphs matter more than listing many quotations.

teach.heading: Model: a paragraph with context
teach.note: I do. Read the answer aloud and then colour-code point, evidence, analysis, context and link. Check the quotation in the class copy. The phrase is from early in the novel, where the narrator explains Okonkwo's character.

model.problem: Explore how Achebe presents fear in Things Fall Apart.
steps: Point: Achebe presents fear as the force that drives Okonkwo.
Evidence: his life is 'dominated by fear', 'the fear of failure and of weakness'.
Zoom: the repetition of 'fear' and the abstract nouns suggest it is a constant, shaping force, rooted in shame about his father.
Context: in Igbo society a man's worth depends on titles and strength, so his fear of weakness is also a social pressure.
Link: this fear later leads to violence and his tragic end.
model.answer: Achebe presents fear as the force that drives Okonkwo. The narrator tells us his life is 'dominated by fear, the fear of failure and of weakness', and the repetition of 'fear' suggests a constant pressure that shapes every choice. Because Igbo society values titles and strength, his fear is also a social pressure, which helps explain why he later turns to violence and meets a tragic end.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Discuss the options. B is the strongest because it includes context and analysis. D is a plot retelling.

check.q: Which paragraph ending is most effective?
options: So that is what happens in the novel.
This fear, shaped by his society, drives his violent choices and so shows the cost of rigid masculinity.
Okonkwo was a man.
In conclusion, there are many themes.
check.why: B links the paragraph back to the question and gives a judgement. The others are summary or vague.

teach.heading: Self-assessment checklist
bullets: A clear argument runs through the whole essay
Evidence is short and integrated
Context is linked to the writer's choices
A conclusion that shows personal judgement
teach.note: Give pupils a checklist and a timed paragraph. Remind them that AO1 and AO4 are the assessment focus here (not AO2 in the same way as poetry), so critical, informed argument matters most. Check the latest mark scheme for the AO split.

practice: Retrieve: list the three parts of a developed paragraph.
Give one theme in your text and a quotation for it.
What is a judgement?
independent: Core: write a plan for the practice question on your text.
Extend: write two developed paragraphs.
Stretch: write a full conclusion with an evaluative judgement.
exit: What should a conclusion do?
Write one integrated quotation.
Big question: what does a high-level essay look like?
lessons.homework: Write the full timed essay on your text (about 45 minutes) and self-assess against the checklist.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a paragraph frame and a model plan. Allow extra time if agreed. Stretch: compare your essay against a partner's and improve one paragraph each.
